newsitem.title: BELGIUM: "Empty" EMU fanciful and impractical, experts say.
newsitem.headline: "Empty" EMU fanciful and impractical, experts say.

text.p: The idea that a single European currency could be launched without any members to preserve the concept while delaying implementation is gaining some ground but is dismissed as fanciful and impractical by many EU officials and analysts.

If the European Union's grand design for economic and monetary union (EMU) has to be delayed beyond 1999, there would have to be a renegotiation of the Maastricht treaty, requiring unanimous ratification by all the blocs 15 nations.

This is the dominant view emerging from conversations with EU monetary officials who strongly deny there is any alternative to a full-scale revision of the treaty -- which officials fear could threaten to undermine the whole project.
There are simply no loopholes, escape clauses or easy manoeuvres around this fact, a reality that makes contemplation of a postponement all the more disquieting.

The monetary officials were commenting on the so-called empty shell approach, a strategy that has captured the attention of some in the financial markets and which sees a formal launch of the single currency in 1999 but with no members participating.
Some say this would in effect avoid a messy and complicated revision of Maastricht and allow countries to join EMU when they are economically fit.
EU officials say there are several problems with this plan, not least the implications for the European Monetary Institute (EMI), forerunner to a European Central Bank (ECB).

"Once you start stage three of monetary union you would have to unwind the EMI. That's what the treaty says. But if you have no members in EMU you could not establish a board for the ECB. Effectively you would have only a president," said one senior EU official.

More importantly, analysts say such an open-ended delay would lack credibility as there would be no new fixed start date. This alone could raise market doubts over the commitm,ent of governments to bring their public finances in line with the treaty.

Among the benefits of a fixed timetable is a degree of certainty for banks and corporations in planning their businesses. Without a date there would be renewed doubts and the potential for confusion and technical problems.
"In the real world where preparations are underway, people would laugh at the prospect of a monetary union with no members," said Graham Bishop, European Adviser at Salomon Brothers in London.
Alternatively, the prospect of a short delay, say for six months, has been floated among EU officials for some time, but for very different reasons.

There has been a longstanding concern that the period between the decision on which countries qualify for EMU -- March or April in 1998 -- and the launch date on January 1, 1999, is too short for the ECB to become fully operational.

In addition, there are worries that the private banking sector might not be adequately prepared. Although large institutions have been quite active in positioning themselves for the changeover, smaller banks are known to be behind.

Under such a scenario analysts say it is conceivable that EU leaders could decide to postpone the single currency's introduction by a few months. But such a technical delay, accompanied by a credible new launch date, is entirely different from the "empty shell" concept.
Experts add that any serious consideration of a delay for more fundamental reasons would not arise until later this year when the economic situation in Europe becomes clearer.
"We really haven't given any thought to this type of artificial construction," said one EU monetary official in commenting on the empty shell strategy.
And while much attention has been focused on Germany's unemployment problem and the impact it has on its budget deficit, some say such a narrow view neglects other important developments.
Among them is the strength of the dollar. The unexpected climb in the U.S. currency in recent months should have a beneficial effect on Europe's economic fortunes.
In addition, the broader economic backdrop within the industrialised world -- stable inflation and low short- and long-term interest rates -- is also a plus for growth.
